Key populations-sensitive health services and programming

Planning, implementation and monitoring tool
About this tool

This interactive planning, implementation and monitoring tool brings together World Health Organization guidance on key populations-sensitive health services and programming. It enables countries and partners to explore recommended interventions, assess reported service availability, identify gaps and support the adaptation of global guidance to national and local contexts.(1,11)

The tool provides a rapid planning assessment and does not replace comprehensive programme review, consultation with communities, national policy processes or context-specific technical guidance.

It is framed around the WHO recommended comprehensive package of essential interventions for people from key populations — men who have sex with men, trans and gender diverse people, sex workers, people who inject drugs, and people in prisons and other closed settings — covering enabling, health (HIV, tuberculosis (TB), viral hepatitis and sexually transmitted infections (STIs)), broader health and supportive interventions(1,2).

It is intended for national programme managers, policy-makers, community-led organizations, implementing partners and funders, who can use it to compare what a country currently offers against WHO recommendations, identify gaps, and see how needs change for people who present intersecting needs from more than one key population(1,18).

Who are considered part of key populations▶

WHO identifies five key populations:

Men who have sex with men (MSM)Trans and gender diverse people (TGD)Sex workers (SW)People who inject drugs (PWID)People in prisons and other closed settings (PPC)

Source: WHO consolidated guidelines for key populations, 2022 (1).

Barriers to care▶
  • Disproportionate burden of HIV, sexually transmitted infections (STIs), viral hepatitis and other conditions(1,14)
  • Criminalization, punitive laws and weak legal protection(1,16)
  • Stigma and discrimination in health settings(19)
  • Violence and unsafe environments(1)
  • Poverty, housing insecurity and exclusion from education and work(16)
Intersecting vulnerabilities▶
  • Belonging to more than one key population(1)
  • Involvement in sex work(1)
  • Alcohol and other substance use, including chemsex(17)
  • Incarceration and the period after release(15)
  • Combined exposure requires tailored prevention and care(1,26)
Disease burden across key populations▶

People from key populations and their partners carry a disproportionate share of HIV, viral hepatitis, tuberculosis and sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and face substantial unmet sexual and reproductive health needs. Select a disease below for detail.(1,11,16)

HIVHIV▶
1.3 millionnew infections, 2024(14)
  • People from key populations and their partners account for about 80% of new infections outside sub-Saharan Africa(13)
  • About 25% of new infections within sub-Saharan Africa(13)
  • 40.8 million people were living with HIV in 2024(14)
  • Most key population members were not reached with basic prevention services(13)
HEPViral hepatitis▶
#1driver of new hepatitis C infections(8)
  • Injecting drug use accounts for the largest share of new hepatitis C infections globally(8)
  • People who inject drugs, people in prisons, sex workers and men who have sex with men are disproportionately affected(8)
  • Hepatitis deaths are rising rather than falling(11)
  • Hepatitis B and C remain leading causes of cirrhosis and liver cancer(10)
TBTuberculosis▶
10 timeshigher burden in prisons(9,15)
  • Driven by overcrowding, poor ventilation, malnutrition and high HIV prevalence(9)
  • TB remains a leading cause of death among people living with HIV(28)
  • Systematic screening and preventive treatment are essential across key populations(25)
  • Transmission in closed settings extends into the wider community on release(15)
STISexually transmitted infections▶
over 1 millioncurable STIs acquired daily(26)
  • The majority are asymptomatic and are missed without routine screening(26)
  • Adult syphilis infections rose to an estimated 8 million in 2022(12,26)
  • Extragenital infections are missed without targeted pharyngeal and rectal testing(1)
  • Antimicrobial resistance in gonorrhoea is a growing threat(26)
SRHSexual and reproductive health▶
350 000cervical cancer deaths, 2022(27,49)
  • Sex workers are frequently overlooked in guidance and services for pregnant and breastfeeding women, despite needing antenatal care, PrEP during pregnancy and breastfeeding, syphilis screening and safe delivery(1,9)
  • 1.1 million pregnant women had syphilis in 2022, resulting in over 390 000 adverse birth outcomes(26)
  • STIs drive infertility, cancers and pregnancy complications, and increase HIV risk(26)
  • Barriers persist to contraception, cervical screening, safe abortion and gender-affirming care(1)
ALLCombined impact▶
2.5 milliondeaths each year(12)
  • HIV, viral hepatitis and STIs combined(12)
  • Burdens overlap and interact syndemically rather than independently(1)
  • Criminalization, stigma, violence and exclusion amplify every burden(2,16)
  • Siloed programmes miss the people at greatest risk(11)
Why key population-sensitive services and programming matter▶

People from key populations often face legal, social and structural barriers that affect their health and access to care. Key population-sensitive services are designed to be accessible, acceptable, equitable and responsive to their needs. WHO recommends rights-based, integrated and person-centred approaches that address both health needs and barriers to service access(1,19). Key population-sensitive services in this tool are organized into four categories: enabling interventions, health interventions, broader health interventions, and supportive interventions.

Guiding principles
People-centredDesigned with and for communities(1).
Rights-basedHuman rights, equality, non-discrimination(19).
Evidence-informedBased on WHO guidance and global evidence(1).
Context-specificAdapt to local needs, systems and capacities(18).
AccountableMonitor progress and improve quality(23).
The WHO response▶

WHO recommends a comprehensive, integrated, people-centred and human rights–based package of services, presented in this tool(1,18).

WHO mandate in this area(31)
  • Set global normative guidance and recommendations for key population health services(1,11)
  • Support countries to adapt and implement that guidance in national programmes(11,18)
  • Monitor the global burden and the coverage of services, and report on progress(23,24)
  • Promote the right to the highest attainable standard of health without discrimination(31,19,16)
  • Convene countries, communities and partners, and support community-led responses(1,11)

Sources

All content is drawn from World Health Organization (WHO) normative guidance and United Nations sources. Every recommendation links to the publication it comes from. This resource consolidates existing guidance and does not create new recommendations.
